claims.text: Adding a small amount of a reactive element such as Y, La, or Ce to a Cr coating can improve its durability on zirconium-alloy cladding.
Reactive-element alloying can reduce interfacial element transport.
Reactive-element alloying can enhance coating integrity.
The intervention is alloying the Cr coating with a reactive element.
Reactive-element alloying causes formation of a reactive-element oxide layer.
The reactive element reacts with oxygen to form a stable oxide layer at the coating-substrate interface.
The interfacial oxide layer reduces Cr-Zr interdiffusion.
The interfacial oxide layer improves coating adhesion.
The modified coating will have improved durability and reduced premature failure under both normal subcritical-water and accident-relevant steam conditions relative to unmodified Cr-coated cladding.
The hypothesis is applicable from 300 to 1200 °C.
The hypothesis is applicable for exposure times up to 1000 hours.
The applicable environments are subcritical water and high-temperature steam.
Alloyed and unalloyed Cr coatings should be compared under normal and accident conditions using oxidation, morphology, adhesion, integrity, and interfacial-composition measurements.
The hypothesis is falsified if the alloyed coating shows no significant durability improvement or shows increased interfacial element transport.
